utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Will the Court Officer please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-5/18-T, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the appearances for the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone. You know me. It is quite clear. With me is Mr. Peter Robinson, my legal adviser, and I believe that there is someone from Mr. Harvey's team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I have separately the appearances for the stand-by counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. VUKAJLOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. On behalf of the standby team, Mr. Eric Tully and Mirjana Vukajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Susanne Elliot, and Iain Reid appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I would now like to ask the representatives of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela to identify themselves by name and title for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MADAH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Haifa Aissami Madah, Ambassador of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and before the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Alfonso D'Santiago, director of Multilateral Treaties of the Ministry of Foreign Relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could also introduce your colleagues who accompany yourselves today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MADAH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. We'll be pleased to do so. We have with us Dr. Jose Gabriel Ponce [phoen], assistant of the Judicial Office of the Ministry for Foreign Relations of Venezuela; further, Mr. Jose Angel Bucarello, assistant minister of the Embassy in the Netherlands; Mr. Milton Mesa [phoen], assistant minister of the Embassy of Venezuela for or vis-a-vis the Netherlands. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. Today, we are holding a hearing to discuss primarily a binding order motion filed by the accused, Mr. Karadzic, on 1st of November, 2010, in which he requests a number of documents from Venezuela relating to the testimony of the upcoming witness, Ambassador Diego Arria which he says are relevant to his case. For the purpose of today's hearing, let us call this motion as "Venezuela Motion." While Venezuela, having been invited to do so twice by this Chamber, eventually responded to the motion on 28th of December, 2010, stating that it was taking necessary steps to locate the required information, no progress has been made since then. Indeed, on 31st of January, 2011, the Chamber invited Venezuela to provide an update on its activities, but did not hear back. Thus, progress has been very slow, and the motion remains pending. Accordingly, the Chamber determined that it would be helpful to hear from the representatives of Venezuela and the accused at an oral hearing. I should note that the accused has also filed another motion for a binding order against the United Nations, requesting certain documents also relating to Ambassador Arria. Let us call this motion, for the purposes of today's hearing, as "UN Motion." As the parties are aware, the United Nations is of the view that it may not disclose some of these documents without breaching the duty of confidentiality it owes to Venezuela, and that the accused should, therefore, seek Venezuela's consent for the release of the documents in the United Nations' possession. The accused has done so, but has received no response from Venezuela on this issue. On 15th of April this year, the Chamber invited the representatives of the United Nations to attend the hearing, but the United Nations indicated that it did not feel this was necessary, and elected, rather, to rely on its written submissions contained in its previous correspondence. Therefore, we are sitting today in the presence of the accused, the Prosecution, the standby counsel, and the representatives of Venezuela. I would like to thank the Venezuelan representatives, on behalf of the Tribunal and this Chamber, for their attendance and their contribution to this hearing. To introduce the Trial Chamber to the representatives of Venezuela, I am Judge O-gon Kwon, Presiding Judge in this case, and to my right is Judge Howard Morrison, and to my left is Judge Melville Baird, and to my far right, Judge Flavia Lattanzi. Before we move into the submissions, there are a few procedural matters that should be addressed. As you know from the scheduling order issued yesterday, following my opening remarks, I will ask the Defence to update us on the progress in relation to his two motions against Venezuela and the United Nations, and we'll then proceed to ask Venezuelan representatives a certain number of questions. Following these questions, the participants will have an opportunity to raise any other issue relating to the two binding order motions that they feel should be covered during this hearing. The next matter I want to deal with is any application for a private or closed-session hearing. Given that many of the filings in relation to this hearing are public and that no notice of objection, pursuant to our Rule, has been filed by Venezuela, we have decided that we will proceed in public session until a specific issue requiring us to go into a private or closed session arises. Therefore, it is for the Venezuelan representatives to notify the Chamber if they believe we have reached that point, and then the Chamber will consider whether a private session is necessary. If the Chamber decides to go into private session, those watching the hearing in the public gallery will not be able to hear what is being said in the courtroom, nor will the hearing be broadcast to the public. In addition, those portions of transcripts that are in private session will not be available to the public. Indeed, only the parties and the state concerned will receive a copy of those portions of the transcript that are in private session. There is one other matter. As you know, the Chamber has invited the Prosecution to attend this hearing. Unless the accused or the Venezuelan representatives request that discussion of a particular issue or document to be heard ex parte, i.e., in the absence of the Prosecution, the Prosecution shall be here throughout the hearing and shall have access to the transcripts of the hearing. I, therefore, would like to know if there are any objections to that from the Venezuelan representatives and/or from the accused. None from the accused. Madam Aissami Madah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MADAH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the part of the Bolivarian of Venezuela, there is no objection whatsoever. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. Then I would like to hear from the Defence first. I take it that it will be Mr. Robinson that will make submissions in relation to these motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could update us as to any progress since your last submission to the Chamber in relation to these two motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say there's been no progress. I don't have anything additional to report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. We received the same communication that you did, that they didn't choose to attend this hearing, and we've had no other communication with them about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Then turning now to Venezuela: As I have said earlier, the progress in relation to the accused's binding order motion and the related matter of consent to disclosure of documents by the United Nations has been very slow. The one response filed by Venezuela was late, and following that the Chamber heard nothing for months, despite several invitations extended to Venezuela to update the Chamber on the progress it was making in relation to the motion. So before we come to the subject-matter of today's hearing, I wonder if the Venezuelan representatives would like to comment on any of these observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MADAH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would like to begin by informing you of the following: The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela greets the honourable tribunal responsible for persecuting those who have committed violations in the area of Yugoslavia in 1991, and we thank you for the opportunity to speak before this Trial Chamber. In that respect, I would like to give the floor to Dr. Alfonso D'Santiago, whom we have already introduced to you before. He is the director of Multilateral Treaties of the Judicial Unit of the ministry in charge of foreign relations of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, who will be presenting the official and formal point of view of my government as regards the subject matter of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would like to read my statement in Spanish. Mr. President, Honourable Judges of the Tribunal, first of all, I would like to say hello on behalf of the Government of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. It's an honour to be at this Tribunal, at this hearing, to inform you on what the Government of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela has done to meet the request to provide documents by the accused, Radovan Karadzic. On behalf of my government, let me give you the arguments of my country. First of all, I would like to state that the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is fully committed to co-operating with this Court, based on general international law and on Article 29 of the Statute of the Tribunal, and this within the limits of Article 54 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In this respect, my government is determined to taking action as soon as possible, voluntarily and based on the principle of good faith --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker be asked to slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. D'Santiago. You are being asked by the interpreters to slow down when reading the document. So if you could repeat from your government is determined to taking actions as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise, Mr. President. So in this respect, my government is determined to taking action as soon as possible, voluntarily and based on the principle of good faith, in the interests of justice. The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela should say that the request of the accused refers to a pretty broad period of time. And in addition to that, it refers to very old documents. Therefore, looking for those documents, finding them, and compiling them has been extremely difficult, because the archives are not the archives we use daily. However, my government is making all the efforts possible to find those documents. We also would like to add that because of the tragedy that Venezuela has undergone because of the heavy rain we had in November 2010, during which over 120.000 people were left homeless, my country has had to devote very valuable human and financial resources to be able to confront this tragedy. So public offices has been used as shelters to temporarily house many of those people. Offices and archives have had to be moved. What I've just said has made it extremely difficult to locate and compile the documents requested by the accused. Moving on to other things regarding the legal aspects of the request, I would like to point out the following: For my country, the request of the accused, in his letter of 18 October 2010, which was addressed to the Embassy of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in The Hague, does not comply with the Rules of Procedure, of Article 54 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, because Mr. Diego Arria, in addition to having been permanent representative of Venezuela at the UN, was also the president of the Security Council during one month. Article 54 bis, which we've mentioned, provides that the applicant should identify, to the extent possible, the documents or the information requested. However, my country considers that the accused's request does not take into account the fact that during March 1992, the documents produced by Ambassador Arria, in his capacity as President of Security Council, does not belong to the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, but belongs to the United Nations. Therefore, the accused's request includes providing documents which do not belong to my country and which my country might not have. Therefore, in our opinion, the requirement of identifying the documents covered by the Article is not complied with. We should also recall that the accused made a similar request to the UN. He requested a broad range of documents produced by Diego Arria, former permanent representative of Venezuela to the United Nations, during the period between January 1st, 1992, and September 1st, 1993. During that period, my country was a non-permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations. And related to this, we should remember that in its response, the international organisation has provided arguments to the Tribunal according to which revealing certain categories of documents could compromise the principle of confidentiality, which is inherent to the decision-making process of the Security Council. That would be the case for documents which are based or which refer to informal consultations. My country is reasonably concerned by providing documents which could make reference to those informal consultations and which could, therefore, violate the principle of confidentiality and undermining the meaning of the Security Council's debates. What I've just said led our authorities to co-ordinate and consult with the UN in order to decide with that organisation the criteria to determine the documents which can be provided to the accused respecting, at the same time, the principle of confidentiality. Mr. President, I am glad to inform you that after these consultations, my country recently reached an agreement with the Legal Affairs Office of the United Nations. Based on the agreement, my country has committed to working with that organisation to identify the documents that may be handed over. Therefore, and because of the importance our country attaches to the requests from the Tribunal, Venezuela has appointed an official who will work closely in New York with the person responsible at the Legal Affairs Office at the UN in order to identify those documents. Mr. President, with that same spirit, the same spirit in which my country has expressed its willingness to co-operate with this Tribunal, and to conclude the search process, the compilation process, and the analysis process of the requested documents, we would like to inform this Tribunal that the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela hopes to meet the request in this procedure in a time-frame which would be between three and five months. Taking into account the arguments which have been submitted, and to conclude, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela considers very respectfully that this Court needs not issue an order to enforce the accused's request, since it is doing everything it can to voluntarily respond to that request. Thank you very much, Mr. President and Judges of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. D'Santiago. Let me be clear in understanding your submission. I just heard that the search process will have been concluded in three to five months from now on. Separate from that, whether the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela will consent to the disclosure of documents in custody of the United Nations, you submitted that as a result of consultation, an appointed official will work within OLA in determining whether or not to disclose the document. How long will that process take? When can we hear from you whether or not you consent to the disclosure of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As Venezuela has said in its statement, at this time Venezuela has started the co-ordination process with the UN to search for the documents. We think the process is divided up into three stages: search, compilation, and analysis of the documents. We believe that that time-period, three to five months, would be the period necessary to provide the documents so we would be co-ordinating with the United Nations before that dead-line is met. As I said, the maximum dead-line to provide the documents would be of five months, just as I said in the statement a few minutes ago. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. D'Santiago. Before we move forward, we may be assisted by hearing from Mr. Tieger, when we would expect to hear Ambassador Diego Arria's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Based on the time-line identified by Dr. D'Santiago, I think that presents no problem. We would not expect the testimony of Mr. Arria until the Srebrenica component of the case, and, therefore, I think the three- to-five-month anticipated period would expire well before his anticipated testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any observation to make in relation to this submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. First of all, we're happy to hear that the Government of Venezuela will be co-operating with the Tribunal and will be providing the documents. And as long as we receive them in enough time in advance before Ambassador Arria's testimony, then that will be okay with us. However, I find that there may be some ambiguities in the way things are proceeding that may cause further delays beyond the three to five months, particularly the issue of consent, so I think that we need to resolve the question of whether or not there are any categories of documents which either Venezuela or the United Nations will not consent or will not produce to us. And we can have those issues litigated well before the three to five months so that finally whatever documents we do receive are received in a timely fashion before the testimony of the ambassador. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I wonder whether we can hear those answers today at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Mr. President. I think also we need to hear from the United Nations. So the issue of disclosing the informal consultations of the Security Council is one that involves both Venezuela and the United Nations. I would note that Ambassador Arria, himself, in his statement, has disclosed those, and I believe that there's good grounds for the United Nations and Venezuela also being willing to disclose those. But until we hear some official position from them, I don't think we're in a position for you to make a decision on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it, Dr. D'Santiago, that it is Venezuela's position that Venezuela will liaise with the United Nations on this issue directly, without involving the Chamber, and then inform the accused and the Chamber of the outcome once the inspection and consultation have been finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you also heard the submission from Mr. Robinson, so could you bear that in mind in having consultation with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we will take into account what the Defence just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether there is any matters to be raised by any of the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador Aissami Madah or Dr. D'Santiago, are there any matters to raise at this moment? Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Venezuela would like to clarify the fact that in many documents and some documents, we've seen that reference is made to Mr. Diego Arria as "Ambassador Arria from Venezuela" or "Ambassador Arria." My government would like to inform the Tribunal that Mr. Arria was ambassador -- Venezuela's ambassador between 1991 and 1993, and he no longer worked for the Foreign Office as of September 1st, 1993. Therefore, the delegation of Venezuela would like to request the Tribunal that it refers to Mr. Arria as "Ex-Ambassador Arria" or "the former representative of Venezuela to the UN." Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just comment that from what we're used to, there's a few titles, when you have them once, they last forever, and "Ambassador" and "General" are some, and we've only been referring to "Ambassador Arria" out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Out of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Out of custom, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. D'Santiago. Three months from now will be the 10th of July, and five months will be the 10th of September. In our Tribunal, we'll have a summer recess until sometime middle of August, so I wonder if the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela could do its best to produce their final report before we resume after the recess; that is, Monday, the 15th of August. That will be about a bit more than four months' time from now on. And if that is not feasible, I would appreciate it very much if Venezuela could produce a progress report at three months' time from now on, i.e., on 10th of July, whether we can expect a report from Venezuela. Would that be possible, Dr. D'Santiago?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's actually two months between now and the middle of July, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm very sorry. I was mistaken. I was carried away, probably. Yes. Let me consult the calendar again. Yes, three months from now is 10th of August, and five months is 10th of October. So whether my -- my statement was whether we could receive the response from Venezuela by 10th of September, and if not feasible, whether we could expect a progress report by 15th of August, when we resume after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regarding your request, the delegation of Venezuela is not in a position to provide an exact reply, but we will make our best efforts to give you a satisfactory response. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So at the minimum, we expect Venezuela to respond or to make a report by 10th of November, which is five months from now. I'm sorry, October. Yes, October, 10th of October. But more than that, we also expect the Venezuelan authorities to expedite their proceedings so much so that they could produce the report by 10th of September. Otherwise -- 10th of September, four months' time. But if that is not feasible, Venezuela should make a progress report on 15th of August. I think we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'SANTIAGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we would do that, Mr. President. We will do what you requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To make things clear, a written order will follow after this hearing. The hearing is now adjourned. Have a nice afternoon. --- The hearing concluded at 4.38 p.m.
